narrative:
The 2026 Texas Rangers opened their season with a promising March, going 4-1 in the early going and flashing the kind of capable roster that had carried them to glory in recent years. But April told a different story — a 11-15 month riddled with late-game collapses, bullpen meltdowns, and costly moments from pitchers Jacob Latz and Chris Martin. The Rangers found themselves underwater almost immediately, chasing the division rather than leading it, and the wounds of those early losses lingered long into the summer.

May offered only modest relief at 13-15, though glimmers of life emerged in the clutch contributions of Jake Burger and Danny Jansen, whose back-to-back singles in mid-May kept faint hopes alive. It was June that finally delivered a genuine surge — a 16-11 month that served as the season's emotional peak, reminding the Globe Life Field faithful that this team had real fight in it. The offense woke up, the lineup found rhythm, and for a stretch it felt like the Rangers might claw their way back into relevance.

July and August, however, ground those hopes down. Cole Winn's continued struggles on the mound gave opponents highlight-reel home runs, and a cumulative run differential that had never fully recovered from April began to drag the team below .500 for good. Bright individual performances from Ezequiel Duran and Wyatt Langford in August kept the games competitive, but the pitching staff's inability to hold late leads — illustrated again and again by Jacob Latz's recurring disasters — meant too many wins slipped away.

September arrived with the Rangers sitting at 67-70 and requiring something close to a miracle to stay relevant. A 12-12 finish was respectable but not enough to move the needle. Jacob Latz's continued late-season implosions and a Jakob Junis home-run surrender in mid-September summed up a year in which the pitching staff simply could not match a lineup that, on its best days, had real pop. At 80-82, the Rangers find themselves staring at a season that promised more than it delivered, their postseason fate hinging on how the rest of the league's final weeks unfold.

chapters.title: False Dawn
chapters.description: An encouraging March gives way to an April defined by bullpen breakdowns and early-inning collapses that set the Rangers behind from the start.

chapters.title: Burger's Lifeline
chapters.description: Jake Burger and Danny Jansen deliver back-to-back clutch hits in May to keep the Rangers treading water as the team searches for an identity.

chapters.title: The June Surge
chapters.description: A 16-11 June stands as the season's high-water mark, giving Rangers fans a genuine reason to believe before the summer heat takes its toll.

chapters.title: Grinding Through Summer
chapters.description: July and August bring a mixed record and flashes of offensive brilliance from Duran and Langford, but the pitching staff's fragility prevents any sustained momentum.

chapters.title: September's Hard Truths
chapters.description: A .500 September and recurring pitching failures from Latz and Junis close out a frustrating 80-82 campaign that fell short of expectations.
